blocks.text: 1.5.4 Switch Patterns in Java (Java 17+)
Concept Explanation

Switch patterns, introduced as a preview feature in Java 17 (JEP 406), refined in Java 18-20 and standard since Java 21 (JEP 441), represent a significant improvement in Java's pattern matching capabilities. This feature extends the switch statement and expression to work with patterns, allowing for more expressive and concise code when dealing with complex data structures and type hierarchies.

Switch patterns enable developers to combine type checking, type casting, and data extraction into a single, readable construct. This feature is particularly useful when working with sealed classes, records, and other hierarchical data structures.
Key Points to Remember

items: Switch patterns work with both switch statements and switch expressions.
They support type patterns, guarded patterns, and null cases.
Pattern variables introduced in case labels are in scope for that case's code block.
The compiler performs exhaustiveness checking for switch expressions and statements with no default clause.
Switch patterns work well with sealed classes and records, providing compile-time safety for exhaustive matching.

blocks.text: Relevant Java Features

items: Introduced as a preview feature in Java 17
Refined in previews in Java 18, 19 and 20; standard in Java 21
Works in conjunction with sealed classes (Java 17+) and records (Java 16+)

blocks.text: Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

items: **Forgetting exhaustiveness**: Ensure all possible cases are covered or include a default case.
**Overlapping patterns**: Be cautious of patterns that may overlap, as the first matching pattern is selected.
**Unintended fall-through**: Unlike traditional switches, pattern cases don't fall through by default.

blocks.text: Best Practices and Optimization Techniques

items: Use switch patterns for type-based dispatching in object-oriented hierarchies.
Combine with sealed classes for compile-time exhaustiveness checking.
Prefer switch expressions over statements for more concise and less error-prone code.
Use guards to add additional conditions to patterns.

blocks.text: Edge Cases and Their Handling

items: Null handling: Explicitly handle null with `case null` (a `default` label alone does not match null).
Subtype relationships: Be aware of the order of cases when dealing with subtypes.

blocks.text: Interview-specific Insights

items: Interviewers may ask about the benefits of switch patterns over traditional instanceof checks and casts.
You might be asked to refactor existing code to use switch patterns for improved readability and maintainability.
Understanding the interaction between switch patterns and sealed classes is crucial.

blocks.text: Q: What are the main benefits of using switch patterns over traditional instanceof checks and casts?
A: Switch patterns offer several advantages over traditional instanceof checks and casts:

items: Conciseness: They combine type checking, casting, and variable binding into a single, readable construct.
Exhaustiveness: The compiler can check if all possible cases are covered, reducing the risk of runtime errors.
Pattern matching: They allow for more complex matching, including nested patterns and guards.
Readability: The code becomes more declarative and easier to understand, especially for complex type hierarchies.
Safety: They eliminate the need for explicit casting, reducing the risk of ClassCastExceptions.

Q: How do switch patterns interact with sealed classes, and why is this interaction important?
A: Switch patterns work particularly well with sealed classes due to their complementary nature:

items: Exhaustiveness checking: Sealed classes define a fixed set of possible subtypes. When used with switch patterns, the compiler can ensure that all possible subtypes are handled, providing compile-time safety.
Pattern matching: Switch patterns can match against the specific subtypes of a sealed class, allowing for type-safe, expressive code.
Extensibility control: Sealed classes restrict which classes can extend them, and switch patterns provide a natural way to handle all permitted subtypes.
Design clarity: The combination encourages clear hierarchies and promotes thinking about all possible cases in the domain model.

Q: Can you explain how guards work in switch patterns and provide an example of their use?

A: Guards in switch patterns allow you to add additional conditions to a case, providing more fine-grained control over pattern matching. They are introduced using the `when` keyword followed by a boolean expression.
Key points about guards:

items: They allow for more specific matching beyond just the type.
Guards are evaluated only if the pattern matches.
They can reference pattern variables introduced in the case label.

Q: How does null handling work with switch patterns, and what are the best practices for dealing with null values?
A: Switch patterns provide explicit support for handling null values. Here are the key points and best practices:

items: Null case: You can explicitly handle null using `case null ->`, or combine it with the default as `case null, default ->`.
Placement: The null case, if present, is often placed first, where a reader sees it immediately.
Exhaustiveness: Null plays no part in exhaustiveness checking; a switch can be exhaustive without `case null`.
Default case: If you don't explicitly handle null, a NullPointerException is thrown for null inputs, whether or not the switch has a default case: `default` never matches null.

blocks.text: Best practices:

items: Always consider null handling in your switch patterns.
Explicitly handle null if it's a valid input in your domain.
If null is not expected, you might omit the null case to fail fast with a NullPointerException.
Use `case null, default ->` to handle both null and any other value in one branch, if appropriate.
